message.content: Quill was the only solid thing in a landscape made of thought. The world had no ground, only drifting planes of color: cerulean waves folding into brick-red rectangles, pale circles dissolving into scribbled grids. There were no trees, no stones, no wind—only the memory of forms waiting to be named. In the middle of this strange field stood a hedgehog no bigger than a teacup, wearing round wire glasses that glinted like tiny silver moons. His spines were the only shadows in a place without darkness. When he moved, the abstract shapes shivered, as if they had never been touched before. Every step Quill took made the impossible world a little easier to understand. He walked through a river of diagonal stripes, and the stripes slowed to let him pass. He crossed a patch of torn canvas where a yellow spiral argued with a black line, and the line bowed low. His glasses kept the world at a respectful distance: he could see the edges, the gaps, the unfinished places where beauty had not yet learned how to hold itself together. The abstract art did not attack him, because there was nothing in it that knew how to attack. It simply rearranged itself around his small, real body, forming a path like a sentence slowly becoming legible. His glasses did not fix the world; they revealed how much it was missing. Through the lenses, Quill saw the hollow center of a great orange circle, the trembling pause between two parallel strokes, the silence hidden inside a burst of green. He understood that the world was not broken. It was unfinished. It was a painting before its final brush, a dream before it chose a face. The more closely he looked, the more the shapes seemed to lean toward him, not as things, but as questions. They had been waiting for someone who could tell whether they were beautiful or merely possible. The abstract world loved him because he was the only one who could prove it existed. At night—or what served as night when a soft gray veil covered every direction—Quill sat beneath a mountain of blue triangles that did not fall because falling required a rule they had not yet invented. He pushed his glasses up his nose and watched the forms settle into one another like sleepers finding room. Somewhere beyond the painted edge, the real world probably continued with rain and road and ordinary birds, but here the only creature with breath and bones had become a point of truth. The abstract art shimmered around him, not because it had become real, but because a hedgehog with glasses had looked at it and, for one small moment, believed in its beauty.
